extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers studying short fiction, horror, and women's contributions to literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and interpretive criteria for reading or writing horror by and about women, emphasizing genre features (interplay of real and fantastic), political/personal dimensions, and the use of gothic tropes and biography. Useful for literary analysis or crafting short-form horror that engages social realities and interior trauma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of factual and fantastical
rubrics_metrics.description: "Horror is one of the only genres that allows for a constantly evolving interplay of the factual and fantastical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the genre's flexibility to blend real-world details with uncanny elements. Examples: Frankenstein as a non-religious creation myth that upended literature; authors can mix believable social realities with invented monstrosity to produce affect and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entering the reader's mind and anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you enter into horror, you're entering into your own mind, your own anxiety, your own fear, your own darkest spaces," (Carmen Maria Machado).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective horror probes interiority and subjective fear; writing should aim to evoke personal, psychological responses. When executed well it can 'unmake' the reader — strive for visceral, intimate emotional impact rather than mere shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blending the personal and the political
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror "increasingly slips between the personal and political, the real and surreal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage horror to explore systemic and social issues through individual experiences. Example: Tananarive Due's remark 'Black history is Black horror' and the reading of Beloved as horror because it renders the horrors of slavery. Use personal narratives to illuminate political realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframing non-horror works via the horror lens
rubrics_metrics.description: The trend is to read works not traditionally labeled horror (e.g., Toni Morrison's Beloved) through a horror lens to foreground real-world atrocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or writing, consider how emphasizing the horrific aspects of trauma or historical violence can recast a text as horror. This approach uncovers social horror embedded in realism or literary fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using horror as a collective frame or shorthand for social fears
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror can offer us a collective frame of reference for our fears and experiences; adaptations (e.g., Gas Light) become shorthand for forms of domestic violence or political manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ familiar tropes and cultural shorthand to make social commentary accessible and resonant. In contemporary contexts (post-#MeToo, post-Trump) horror imagery and metaphors help articulate shifting social realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraying behind-the-scenes, real-life abuses and trauma
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror can depict off-page/behind-the-camera horrors (e.g., child actors' abuse) that are as horrific as invented monsters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write or analyze horror that surfaces real institutional or interpersonal abuses. Example: The Monster of Her Age uses the filming experience and family disbelief to show trauma; emphasize consequences like not being believed and long-term anguish rather than supernatural spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using gothic tropes to replay memory and abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic tropes and style can be used to replay physical and emotional abuse within the walls of the mind and memories (Carmen Maria Machado's approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply gothic conventions (haunted houses, memory-as-haunting, atmosphere) to dramatize psychological harm. This is a method for rendering internal trauma as externalized, haunting imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial biography as a source of horror themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial life events can inform horror — Mary Shelley's personal losses and social marginalization shaped Frankenstein's themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or critiquing horror, consider how an author's biography and historical context supply source material and thematic resonance. Biographical detail can legitimize certain motifs (birth/death, isolation, social stigma) and deepen the story's emotional stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror's ethical/representational potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror can 'reflect women and women's realities back to themselves' and be a mode for telling personal stories (e.g., queer domestic violence in In the Dream House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use horror responsibly to represent marginalized experiences; prioritize authenticity and the ethical depiction of trauma. Horror can validate and make visible experiences often minimized or disbelieved.
